notes:
I've put together notes for 2 Samuel 14 below. The sources were mostly Guzik (Enduring Word), Precept Austin, Matthew Henry, Gill, Ellicott, the Pulpit Commentary, Spurgeon, MacLaren, Constable and Kelly. Three gaps up front:

- **Protestant traditions:** I didn't find any real disagreement between denominations on this chapter. Every Protestant teacher I read reads verse 14 as pointing to the gospel. Where commentators do differ, it's on smaller points, and those are marked "Differing views."
- **Catholic, Orthodox and modern scholarship:** I didn't read any newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org or bibleodyssey.org pages, or any netbible.org translator's notes. The only views I have from those directions are a Catholic translation of verse 14 and a few scholarly points quoted by Protestant writers.
- **Popular modern teaching:** I found nothing on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace readings of this chapter, so that category is left out.

---

**v. 1:** Guzik thinks Joab, fiercely loyal to David, may have acted to protect him, judging it dangerous to leave Absalom brooding abroad. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-14/
- Wiersbe (quoted by Precept Austin) says Joab wanted a crown prince ready in case something happened to David, who was now nearly sixty. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-14-commentary
- MacArthur (also quoted there) says fear of public opinion held David back from pardoning his son. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-14-commentary
- *Differing views:* Precept Austin reports that Keil & Delitzsch read the verse negatively: Joab saw the king's heart was *against* Absalom. Almost all modern translations read it positively, though Precept Austin notes that verse 24 gives the negative reading some support. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-14-commentary

**vv. 2–3:**
- Tekoa was about ten miles south of Jerusalem, Amos's hometown, and about five miles from Bethlehem, Joab's birthplace, so he may have heard of this woman. Precept Austin https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-14-commentary
- Here "wise" is the same Hebrew word used for Jonadab in 13:3, but in a good sense rather than "shrewd." Joab was copying Nathan's method from 12:1–7, using a made-up story. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-14-commentary
- Matthew Henry: the story was set far from Jerusalem so David wouldn't wonder why he hadn't already heard of the case.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-samuel/14-14.html
- *Differing views on motive:* Kelly (Brethren) says Joab knew David's conscience was troubled, because God had trusted him with the sword of justice and Absalom had stained the land with blood.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-samuel/14-14.html
- Kingcomments also contrasts this with Nathan: Nathan wanted to wake David's conscience, while this woman wanted him to switch it off and let Absalom back without justice being done.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/2-samuel-14.html

**v. 4:**
- In Israel, people who felt their local judges had treated them unfairly could take their case to the king. Guzik https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/archives/guzik_david/StudyGuide2017-2Sa/2Sa-14.cfm
- "Help" is the Hebrew *yasha'* ("save, deliver"), the root behind the name Yeshua/Jesus. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-14-commentary

**v. 5:**
- The Treasury of Scripture Knowledge (quoted by Precept Austin) suggests the main details may have been real, with Joab finding someone whose life resembled the case. It adds that Josephus says she was elderly. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-14-commentary

**v. 6:** Precept Austin sees this as murder, but presumably not planned, like Cain and Abel. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-14-commentary

**v. 7:**
- Guzik explains the "avenger of blood" custom. The cities of refuge (Numbers 35) protected someone guilty of manslaughter until the case could be heard properly. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-14/
- The "ember" image: households lit the morning fire from the last coal of the night before. Losing her last son would end her husband's name. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-14-commentary

**v. 9:**
- Precept Austin: her words imply she had put David in an awkward position by asking him to free a killer, so she offers to carry the blame herself.  https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-14-commentary

**vv. 10–11:**
- She wanted an oath, because swearing by God's name would bind David to his word. Precept Austin https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-14-commentary
- Guzik: with this oath David put family sympathy ahead of justice and neglected his duty as Israel's chief judge. He quotes Redpath: "He guaranteed safety at the expense of justice, and immediately the farsighted woman captured him in her trap." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-14/
- Matthew Henry sees differences between the cases. Absalom killed out of an old grudge, at a feast in front of guests, not in a sudden fight in the field.  Unlike her son, Absalom was not the only heir.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Sa/2Sa_014.cfm

**v. 12:** With the trap sprung, she now draws out the story's hidden meaning, much as Nathan did with "You are the man!" Precept Austin https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-14-commentary

**v. 13:**
- It took courage to say this, since ancient kings could execute people for the smallest offence. Precept Austin https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-14-commentary
- Constable: her references to "the people of God" suggest popular support for Absalom's pardon.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-samuel/14-14.html
- Guzik says she was confronting David's failure to start the reconciliation himself. He quotes Clarke: David would pardon a poor widow's son but not his own, whom the whole nation wanted back. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-14/

**v. 14 (the key verse):**
- *The urgency point:* Guzik says she was pressing urgency on David: once we die, the chance to reconcile is gone. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-14/
- *Gospel reading (shared across Protestant traditions):*
  - Guzik calls this one of the best gospel texts in the Old Testament. God reconciles us by satisfying justice, not ignoring it, through Christ bearing the punishment on the cross. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-14/
  - Spurgeon (Baptist): despite His greatness, God uses His wisdom to find ways to bring guilty, banished people back.  He also urges hearers to find ways to bring back those they themselves have shut out.  https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/means-for-restoring-the-banished
  - MacLaren (Baptist): "banished" and "expelled" are the same Hebrew word, so the sense is that God makes ways for the banished to stop being banished.  He also says the woman's comparison breaks down. She was asking David to set the law aside by decree, while God "devising means" shows He cannot pardon by a mere act of will.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/maclaren_alexander/expositions-of-holy-scripture/2-samuel/gods-banished-ones.cfm
  - A sermon collected on Bible Hub (Cadman) links the verse to the cities of refuge, where an accidental killer could go home after the high priest died.  https://biblehub.com/sermons/2_samuel/14-14.htm
  - Gill makes the same cities-of-refuge link.  https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/esv/2-samuel/14-14.html
  - Matthew Henry says she was appealing to God's mercy toward guilty sinners.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-samuel/14-14.html
- *A note of caution:*
  - Another sermon in the same Bible Hub collection says her argument was clever reasoning that won because it appealed to the heart rather than the head.  https://biblehub.com/sermons/2_samuel/14-14.htm
  - Kelly, by contrast, says David could not resist the argument: if God makes ways to bring back His banished, who was David to refuse?  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-samuel/14-14.html
- *Translation differences:*
  - The KJV reads "neither doth God respect any person," while the NET and others read "God does not take away life."  https://biblehub.com/2_samuel/14-14.htm
  - The Good News Translation goes another way: even God doesn't raise the dead, but the king can at least bring a man back from exile.  https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/esv/2-samuel/14-14.html
  - The Catholic Douay-Rheims renders it as God not wanting a soul to perish, but calling back the one cast off.  https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/esv/2-samuel/14-14.html
- Precept Austin: "God does not take away life" alludes to God's mercy in sparing sinners, which David had experienced himself when Nathan told him he would not die (12:13).  https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-14-commentary

**vv. 15–16:**
- Here she returns to her own story.  https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-14-commentary
- MacArthur: the relatives hunting her son stand for the people David feared, who resented Absalom and would oppose a pardon.  https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-14-commentary

**v. 17:**
- Precept Austin calls "like the angel of God" exaggeration, perhaps to win favour. It thinks a reference to the Angel of the LORD (as the New Jerusalem Bible's capital letters suggest) is unlikely.  https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-14-commentary
- The Pulpit Commentary takes it to mean the king will hear both sides calmly and judge rightly.  https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-14-commentary

**vv. 18–19:**
- David shows real discernment in spotting Joab behind it. Joab had probably got her in to see the king and may have stayed in the room.  https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-14-commentary
- Matthew Henry reads her admission as: if it was well done, thank Joab; if badly, blame him.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-samuel/14-14.html

**v. 20:**
- Clarke calls this typical Eastern flattery.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-samuel/14-20.html
- Precept Austin says she goes "over the top" in claiming David knows everything on earth.  https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-14-commentary

**vv. 21–22:**
- Joab's words "the request of his servant" suggest he had asked for Absalom's return before. Precept Austin https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-14-commentary
- Guzik: Joab got what he thought was best for Israel and hoped it would prevent a rebellion. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-14/

**v. 23:** Geshur lay north-east of the Sea of Galilee. Joab wasted no time. Precept Austin https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/64081/

**v. 24:**
- Guzik: having been too soft with his sons before (13:21), David now overcorrects into harshness, which can provoke children to anger (Ephesians 6:4). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-14/
- Matthew Henry says he can't see how David could be excused for suspending the law of Genesis 9:6 ("whoever sheds man's blood...").  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Sa/2Sa_014.cfm
- Bible Hub notes that the Hebrew word for "return" (*shuv*) often implies repentance, which is missing in Absalom's case.  https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/2_samuel/14.htm
- *Differing views on David:*
  - Kelly reads this positively: David was not indifferent to past guilt.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-samuel/14-14.html
  - Constable: David's forgiveness was official but not personal.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-samuel/14-28.html
  - F. B. Meyer says the opposite of Henry: David let Absalom back without a word of confession, and the king was overruled by the father.  https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-14-commentary

**v. 25:**
- Guzik: Absalom's looks help explain his popularity, just as Israel was drawn to the handsome Saul. Absalom was probably now crown prince, since Amnon was dead and Chileab is never heard of again. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-14/
- Bible Hub warns against valuing outward appearance over inner character.  https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/2_samuel/14.htm

**v. 26:**
- Guzik puts the yearly haircut at about five and a half pounds. He quotes Redpath: Absalom was proud of his hair and lost his life because of it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-14/
- Bible Hub also sees the hair as foreshadowing his death (18:9).  https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/2_samuel/14.htm

**v. 27:**
- *Usual view:* the sons died young. That's why they're unnamed, and why Absalom later says "I have no son" (18:18).
  - Ellicott, Poole, the Cambridge Bible, the Pulpit Commentary and Keil & Delitzsch all take this view.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/14-27.htm
  - Matthew Henry gives the reverse order: he thinks Absalom built the pillar before his children were born.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Sa/2Sa_014.cfm
- *Scholarly view:* Walter Kaiser (quoted by Precept Austin) notes that some scholars see an unsolvable conflict between 14:27 and 18:18. Kaiser himself argues that early childhood death is the only explanation that fits all the evidence.  https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-14-commentary
- *Tamar:*
  - Guzik: Absalom named his daughter after his wronged sister. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-14/
  - The Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) adds that she married Rehoboam. Ellicott calls this a confused note. The Cambridge Bible suggests the queen Maachah was actually Absalom's granddaughter, through Tamar and Uriel.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_samuel/14-27.htm

**v. 28:**
- Laney: over these two years the seed of bitterness grew, and it later bore fruit in rebellion.  https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-14-commentary
- Coffman: Absalom's pride was not humbled. He was angry at losing his place at court, not grateful to be alive.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-samuel/14-28.html

**v. 29:**
- Matthew Henry thinks Joab stayed away because Absalom hadn't been properly grateful, since proud men treat every favour as owed to them.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Sa/2Sa_014.cfm
- He adds that a truly repentant Absalom would have welcomed the quiet away from court.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Sa/2Sa_014.cfm

**vv. 30–31:**
- Guzik: burning the field shows how brutal and amoral Absalom was, the opposite of the humble, repentant prodigal son. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-14/
- Spurgeon (quoted by Guzik) applies it devotionally: sometimes God "sets our barley-field on fire" to get our attention. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-14/
- *Differing views:* in his own exposition, Spurgeon describes Absalom as sincerely wanting his old honours back, which is a gentler reading.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/2-samuel-14.html

**v. 32:** Guzik: "if there is iniquity in me" shows Absalom felt fully justified, since he saw himself as having punished his sister's rapist. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-14/

**v. 33:**
- Guzik: David forgave without repentance and, as chief judge, overlooked obvious crimes. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-14/
  - He quotes Trapp: David "should have kicked him rather; and not have hardened him to further villainy."
  - He quotes Redpath: David's forgiveness was inadequate and led to more sin, while God's forgiveness is complete and deters further sin. 
- Precept Austin's source calls the meeting a nice ritual, but without a forgiving spirit.  https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/64081/
- Bible Hub notes the Hebrew word for "kiss" can mean either affection or a formal gesture of peace.  https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/2_samuel/14.htm
